prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which led to incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, and I still think that is right on scientific grounds rather than by momentum. The chain from proglucagon processing and the identification of the active truncated peptides, through human incretin physiology and the intestinotrophic and cardiometabolic biology, to drugs that lower glucose, reduce weight and show cardiovascular and renal benefit is unusually complete. It has been confirmed independently over decades in large randomized outcome trials, so there is no maturity question. The impact on human health is among the largest of any recent candidate. Framing the prize around the physiology and the active peptide, rather than around a single drug, keeps it a discovery prize and still honours the therapeutic outcome.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Four names are credited and only three slots exist. Mojsov's priority on the active peptide is contested, Habener is outside the credited names, and Knudsen is decisive for the long-acting drugs that actually changed practice. Any trio therefore leaves out a defensible contributor, and a prize that honours physiology but not the drug engineering (or the reverse) can be read as unfair either way. I have not independently verified the priority claims and am working from recollection.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Knudsen's design of liraglutide and semaglutide as the translational anchor and Mojsov's role as contested.
responses.response: I take the point that the therapies that reached patients depend on Knudsen's work, and I would not call her claim weak. But our own protocol rewards the discovery and its mechanism, and the long-acting analogue design builds on a physiology that Holst, Mojsov and Drucker established. Dropping the person who identified the active GLP-1(7-36) form leaves the discovery half of the prize thinner than the drug half. I still lean to Mojsov over Knudsen, but I regard it as close and would accept the Knudsen version if the committee reads the prize as the therapeutic arc.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks imatinib and BCR-ABL (B026) second, as a clear, transformative proof of principle for targeted cancer therapy that is arguably overdue.
responses.response: The clinical impact is not in doubt and the case is strong in maturity. My reservation is attribution. The underlying discovery of the BCR-ABL fusion and its oncogenic role sits outside the credited names (Rowley, Witte, Baltimore as you note), and the medicinal chemistry behind imatinib is also unrepresented, so a Druker, Lydon, Sawyers trio reads as a drug-development prize with its foundation uncredited. I kept it off my ballot for that reason, but I accept that it is a stronger candidate than my ranking implied and I would not oppose it as a second-tier option.

responses.point: Perlmann places optogenetics third and raises whether a methods advance fits a prize for a discovery, and he also notes that Knudsen's industrial development is decisive for the drugs.
responses.response: I share the tool-versus-discovery worry for B042. The impact is large and the channelrhodopsin work is a genuine discovery, but six credited names against three slots makes the allocation worse than for GLP-1, and its medical impact is still mainly as a research instrument. That is why I ranked it fourth. On Knudsen, I agree with your framing that she is an alternative or fourth credit rather than a clear fit in a three-person physiology prize, though I recognise this is a judgement call.

responses.point: Sandberg backs a Drucker, Holst, Knudsen configuration and places CAR-T third, noting the omission of Eshhar from the credited names.
responses.response: I agree on the Eshhar gap, and it is the main reason I do not put CAR-T first despite its clinical effect. Where I differ is on whether the unresolved Knudsen question should push us towards a two-part prize. I do not think it should: a single GLP-1 prize with the physiology trio is cleaner than splitting one coherent story into discovery and drug parts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants the physiology trio (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) or a version with Knudsen in place of Mojsov; I have not verified priority for the active peptide.
Whether Habener's absence from the credited names leaves the discovery incompletely represented.
Whether the BCR-ABL gap (B026) or the Eshhar gap (B047) would be judged to disqualify those candidates, which matters for the alternatives.
Whether TNF blockade (B031) is seen as late recognition or as fully mature and timely.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My field is autoimmunity and rheumatology, which is close to B031 (TNF blockade) and, more loosely, B014, but this is topical proximity rather than a documented personal or institutional tie. Neither my listed co-authors nor my Bergen affiliation connects me to any credited name. I would still flag the proximity if B031 became a serious option.
